records.text: The COMPASS Lab of the Department of Aerospace Science and Technology - Politecnico di Milano at Politecnico di Milano is thrilled to have participated in the 2026 AAS/AIAA Astrodynamics Specialist Conference, held in Whistler, Canada. The conference brought together leading researchers from around the world in the field of #Astrodynamics , covering topics such as trajectory design and optimisation, spacecraft guidance, navigation and control, proximity operations, #SpaceDebris , and many others. The lab was represented by PhD students Alessandro Michelazzi , Eduardo Polli and Wiebke Retagne , who delivered oral presentations on the following topics: • “Adaptive GNSS-Based #RelativeNavigation for Close #FormationFlying Under Continuous Low-Thrust” - Alessandro Michelazzi , Gabriella Gaias , Camilla Colombo • “ #CollisionAvoidanceManoeuvre Design Under Operational Constraints Using Reaction Control Thrusters” - Eduardo Polli , Juan Luis Gonzalo Gómez , Camilla Colombo • “Generational Evolution of #ExplosionProbability : Investigating the Influence of #MitigationMeasures ” - Wiebke Retagne , Andrea Muciaccia , Camilla Colombo Pre-print versions of the papers are available through the conference website: https://lnkd.in/ejrccH5h Their work was supported by the #GREENSPECIES project, funded by the European Research Council (ERC) , and the Space It Up! project, funded by the Agenzia Spaziale Italiana and the Ministero dell'Università e della Ricerca .

records.title: Ryan Augsburger
records.text: Ohio has the third-largest manufacturing workforce in the nation: nearly 690,000 Ohioans making the products the world depends on. That strength has been generations in the making. Two bicycle makers in Dayton taught the world to fly. Akron put the world on tires. Cleveland and the Mahoning Valley forged the steel that built America’s cities. And Marysville became home to the first Japanese automaker to build cars in the United States. Today, Ohio is putting that experience to work on what comes next. The same skilled workforce, deep supply chains and problem-solving culture now power the industries shaping the future: • Automotive and mobility • Healthcare and biotechnology • Aerospace and defense • Energy • Semiconductors and microelectronics • Food and agriculture …and much more. It’s why the largest capital investment, largest new-jobs project and largest aviation project in state history, from Intel , Anduril Industries and Joby Aviation , all chose Ohio. Here, you can dream it, build it, test it, and scale it. All October, we’re joining The Ohio Manufacturers'​ Association and manufacturers across the state to celebrate #ManufacturingMonth , honoring the people who built Ohio’s legacy and the innovators writing its next chapter. records.title: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: A founder pitch I hear constantly: "our model runs at X frames per second and Y% accuracy." Almost nobody opens with how much bandwidth they actually have to work with — and that
records.text: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: A founder pitch I hear constantly: "our model runs at X frames per second and Y% accuracy." Almost nobody opens with how much bandwidth they actually have to work with — and that number decides more about the architecture than the model does. The chain most people skip: the comms link available to your vehicle — kbps over a contested beyond-line-of-sight SATCOM path versus Mbps over a clean line-of-sight mesh — sets how much you can offload to a human or ground station versus how much has to run onboard. That sets your onboard compute budget. That sets your SWaP class, which determines which sensor packages and vehicle sizes are even physically possible. And SWaP class is what actually determines which program you're a realistic fit for, long before anyone reads your capability statement. A perception stack designed assuming a fat, reliable downlink doesn't just perform worse when the link degrades — it's often not architecturally capable of running any other way, because the onboard/offboard split was never really a design decision, just a default. Here's the trap: the vehicles that lean hardest on that assumption look the most capable in a clean demo. Big model, high frame rate, rich sensor fusion — because none of it had to survive on a starved link. Then the link degrades, contested or just congested, and the gap between "worked in the demo" and "works in the tasking" shows up all at once, in front of the customer. If you haven't written your bandwidth budget down as an explicit number — not "assume good comms," an actual kbps figure for the worst case you're willing to be tested against — you've made an architecture decision by accident. Better to make it on purpose. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

records.title: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: A team I worked with chased a perception fusion bug for two weeks. The lidar returned a clean point cloud. The camera returned a clean detection. Individually, both sensors perfor
records.text: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: A team I worked with chased a perception fusion bug for two weeks. The lidar returned a clean point cloud. The camera returned a clean detection. Individually, both sensors performed exactly to spec. Fused together, the vehicle's obstacle map kept ghosting — objects appearing, shifting eleven centimeters, then reappearing a few feet away. The bug wasn't in either sensor. It was in the extrinsic calibration — the rigid transform describing where each sensor sits relative to the vehicle's reference frame. That transform had been measured once, on a bench, before the vehicle ever left the shop. After a week of field testing — vibration, a few hard stops, one rougher-than-planned landing — one mount had rotated by a fraction of a degree. Invisible to the eye. Invisible on a close-range bench check. But rotational error doesn't behave like translational error. A pure positional shift between two sensors stays roughly constant no matter how far away the target is. A rotational shift scales directly with range — a fifth of a degree of tilt is nothing at arm's length and eleven centimeters of disagreement at thirty meters. That's exactly the kind of drift a bench calibration at close range will never catch, and a mid-range operational test will always find. Individually-passing sensors don't buy you a passing fusion stack. The fix wasn't algorithmic — it was adding an online extrinsic self-check that flags when the sensors' overlapping field of view stops agreeing, before it becomes an obstacle-avoidance decision. Small businesses building perception stacks should treat that self-check as a requirement, not a nice-to-have. It's usually the difference between a DT&E finding you catch yourself and one the government catches for you. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

records.title: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: SBIR/STTR came back in April after a six-month lapse. The new Strategic Breakthrough Phase II awards can reach $30M, but you have to bring a 100% match from private capital or gov
records.text: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: SBIR/STTR came back in April after a six-month lapse. The new Strategic Breakthrough Phase II awards can reach $30M, but you have to bring a 100% match from private capital or government sources. Most founders will read that as a fundraising problem. Its an architecture problem first. Whoever writes the matching cheque will ask the same questions a program office would: (1) Is the autonomy behavior separable from the vehicle? A stack hard-wired to one airframes flight controller is a single-platform product. A stack behind a stable vehicle-interface layer can be sold on many platforms. (2) Are the interfaces stable? If every new integration means changing your perception-to-planning boundary, your Phase II cost curve wont stay flat. (3) What does it do when the world stops matching the demo? Degraded sensors, lost links and out-of-distribution scenes should already be characterized, with data. (4) Where does your IP boundary sit? If the value is in the model weights, the training data and the test harness, can you say who holds rights to each? A component with a good demo is a Phase I story. A $30M award means a system with a defined interface, a characterized failure envelope and a clear IP boundary. Start building those before you write the proposal. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

records.title: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: The Army's Common Autonomous Multi-Domain Launcher (CAML) award went out August 31 — $33.4M, roughly a three-year OTA, to Georgia Tech Research Institute. Not Lockheed, not RTX, n
records.text: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: The Army's Common Autonomous Multi-Domain Launcher (CAML) award went out August 31 — $33.4M, roughly a three-year OTA, to Georgia Tech Research Institute. Not Lockheed, not RTX, not Northrop. GTRI is the Weapon Systems Integrator. That's a more interesting choice than it looks. CAML's architecture decouples the autonomous mobility platform from the munitions pallet — you can swap what it fires without redesigning how it moves. That only works if someone owns the interface control documents independent of whoever builds either half. Normally that someone is a prime with decades of vertical-integration leverage. Here it's a research institute whose job is systems engineering, M&S, and acceptance testing — not building either module itself. For a small business building a mobility platform or a munitions pallet for multi-domain fires, this matters more than the dollar figure. The company you have to satisfy technically here isn't your competitor — it's GTRI, judging whether your module's interface conforms to spec. That's a different relationship than the one you're used to with a prime. Before you map the org chart, find out who owns the interface control documents: that's who actually evaluates your product, and they're grading interface compliance, not just capability. Lt. Gen. Frank Lozano put it plainly: CAML gives the Army "a pathway to experiment with modular launcher concepts, learn quickly, and make informed decisions at the speed of relevance." Still prototype-stage, no production commitment — which means the interface architecture is exactly what's being tested right now. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy #MOSA

records.text: Организация Archer поделилась обновлением: Air traffic control (ATC) still runs on one of the oldest live communication mediums: bandwidth-limited AM radio, spoken in rapid, dense phraseology, where every instruction vanishes the moment it is heard. As a pilot, I witness the operational challenges that come with ATC communications firsthand. Today we're publishing a deep dive into the speech capability of ZEE, Archer's proprietary aviation foundation model. General-purpose models struggle with harsh radio acoustics and restricted jargon, and are unable to understand the nuances of aviation navigational terminology. For example the word "stick" near San Francisco is the SSTIK departure, while "stick" in North Carolina is spelled as STIKK. That nuance is not in the audio, and decoding that signal requires more than just good speech recognition. So we built ZEE differently: — A single speech engine that collapses voice activity detection, speaker diarization, and transcription into one model, emitting one speaker-attributed token stream. — Spatial grounding that injects location context so the model correctly transcribes local waypoints and procedures in any airspace. — A language model that decomposes each dense transmission into discrete, structured, verifiable commands. The result: 84% better accuracy than general-purpose speech models on aviation audio, and a 58% reduction in entity transcription errors from spatial grounding. All of it running in real time, offline, and on-device; so that pilots and controllers alike can benefit from this layer of intelligence. Every radio call becomes a permanent, scrollable, time-indexed record. And it lays the foundation for what comes next: catching readback errors and communication breakdowns in real time, before a misheard clearance becomes an incident. The next era of aviation safety should begin where it matters most: in cockpits and air traffic control towers. Preventing tragic, avoidable accidents starts by making communication clear and effortless in the sky. This is one of the missions behind ZEE, and behind everything my extraordinary team builds: a world where every single flight reaches its destination safely. Full post: https://lnkd.in/dvauVg2E.

records.text: Организация Department of Aerospace Science and Technology - Politecnico di Milano разместила контент: How closely do particles follow rotor-induced flow before reaching a blade? New research by Francesco Caccia and Alberto Guardone investigates the dynamics of inertial particles in rotor-induced flows, considering both a wind turbine and a small-scale propeller. The study shows that the key lies in how the particle response time compares with the characteristic time scale of the induced flow. The authors introduce an induction Stokes number to identify the transition between particles that follow the induced velocity field and those that are essentially unaffected by it. A reduced-order analytical model is then developed to capture this delayed particle response, providing corrected conditions for 2-D sectional simulations and reproducing the transition observed in full 3-D simulations. The results have implications for modelling multiphase rotor flows, including applications involving icing and particle-induced erosion. Read On particle dynamics in steady axial rotor flows, published in the Journal of Fluid Mechanics: https://lnkd.in/eys6i2qJ #AerospaceEngineering #Polimi.

Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: A founder pitch I hear constantly: "our model runs at X frames per second and Y% accuracy." Almost nobody opens with how much bandwidth they actually have to work with — and that number decides more about the architecture than the model does. The chain most people skip: the comms link available to your vehicle — kbps over a contested beyond-line-of-sight SATCOM path versus Mbps over a clean line-of-sight mesh — sets how much you can offload to a human or ground station versus how much has to run onboard. That sets your onboard compute budget. That sets your SWaP class, which determines which sensor packages and vehicle sizes are even physically possible. And SWaP class is what actually determines which program you're a realistic fit for, long before anyone reads your capability statement. A perception stack designed assuming a fat, reliable downlink doesn't just perform worse when the link degrades — it's often not architecturally capable of running any other way, because the onboard/offboard split was never really a design decision, just a default. Here's the trap: the vehicles that lean hardest on that assumption look the most capable in a clean demo. Big model, high frame rate, rich sensor fusion — because none of it had to survive on a starved link. Then the link degrades, contested or just congested, and the gap between "worked in the demo" and "works in the tasking" shows up all at once, in front of the customer. If you haven't written your bandwidth budget down as an explicit number — not "assume good comms," an actual kbps figure for the worst case you're willing to be tested against — you've made an architecture decision by accident. Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: A team I worked with chased a perception fusion bug for two weeks. The lidar returned a clean point cloud. The camera returned a clean detection. Individually, both sensors performed exactly to spec. Fused together, the vehicle's obstacle map kept ghosting — objects appearing, shifting eleven centimeters, then reappearing a few feet away. The bug wasn't in either sensor. It was in the extrinsic calibration — the rigid transform describing where each sensor sits relative to the vehicle's reference frame. That transform had been measured once, on a bench, before the vehicle ever left the shop. After a week of field testing — vibration, a few hard stops, one rougher-than-planned landing — one mount had rotated by a fraction of a degree. Invisible to the eye. Invisible on a close-range bench check. But rotational error doesn't behave like translational error. A pure positional shift between two sensors stays roughly constant no matter how far away the target is. A rotational shift scales directly with range — a fifth of a degree of tilt is nothing at arm's length and eleven centimeters of disagreement at thirty meters. That's exactly the kind of drift a bench calibration at close range will never catch, and a mid-range operational test will always find. Individually-passing sensors don't buy you a passing fusion stack. The fix wasn't algorithmic — it was adding an online extrinsic self-check that flags when the sensors' overlapping field of view stops agreeing, before it becomes an obstacle-avoidance decision. Small businesses building perception stacks should treat that self-check as a requirement, not a nice-to-have. It's usually the difference between a DT&E finding you catch yourself and one the government catches for you. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

The new Strategic Breakthrough Phase II awards can reach $30M, but you have to bring a 100% match from private capital or government sources. Most founders will read that as a fundraising problem. Its an architecture problem first. Whoever writes the matching cheque will ask the same questions a program office would: (1) Is the autonomy behavior separable from the vehicle? A stack hard-wired to one airframes flight controller is a single-platform product. A stack behind a stable vehicle-interface layer can be sold on many platforms. (2) Are the interfaces stable? If every new integration means changing your perception-to-planning boundary, your Phase II cost curve wont stay flat. (3) What does it do when the world stops matching the demo? Degraded sensors, lost links and out-of-distribution scenes should already be characterized, with data. (4) Where does your IP boundary sit? If the value is in the model weights, the training data and the test harness, can you say who holds rights to each? A component with a good demo is a Phase I story. Not Lockheed, not RTX, not Northrop. GTRI is the Weapon Systems Integrator. That's a more interesting choice than it looks. CAML's architecture decouples the autonomous mobility platform from the munitions pallet — you can swap what it fires without redesigning how it moves. That only works if someone owns the interface control documents independent of whoever builds either half. Normally that someone is a prime with decades of vertical-integration leverage. Here it's a research institute whose job is systems engineering, M&S, and acceptance testing — not building either module itself. For a small business building a mobility platform or a munitions pallet for multi-domain fires, this matters more than the dollar figure. The company you have to satisfy technically here isn't your competitor — it's GTRI, judging whether your module's interface conforms to spec. That's a different relationship than the one you're used to with a prime. Before you map the org chart, find out who owns the interface control documents: that's who actually evaluates your product, and they're grading interface compliance, not just capability. Lt. Gen. Frank Lozano put it plainly: CAML gives the Army "a pathway to experiment with modular launcher concepts, learn quickly, and make informed decisions at the speed of relevance." Still prototype-stage, no production commitment — which means the interface architecture is exactly what's being tested right now. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy #MOSA
